newsitem.title: FRANCE: Writer Genevieve Brisac wins French Femina prize.
newsitem.headline: Writer Genevieve Brisac wins French Femina prize.

text.p: France's literary season kicked off on Monday when French writer Genevieve Brisac won the Femina prize for her fourth novel, the tragic tale of a single mother fighting for custody of her son.
Jacqueline Harpman of Belgium and Frenchman Jean Rolin shared the Medicis book prize, also awarded on Monday.
The Femina, awarded by an all-female jury of literati, is France's second-highest literary honour, after the Goncourt prize which will be given next week.

Brisac, 45, won the Femina for her novel "Un Weekend de Chasse a la Mere" -- literally "A Weekend Hunting Mother" -- which is set in Paris and contrasts childhood innocence with the calculation of adults.
Harpman, 67, a psychoanalyst living in Brussels, and Rolin, 47, shared the Medicis for their respective novels "Orlanda" and "The Organisation".
In "Orlanda", Harpman tells the story of a woman who takes on the conscience and body of a man.
"The Organisation", largely an autobiographical work, depicts a group of Maoist students in the 1970s who work in factories.
The Femina jury decided in 1993 to break with tradition and open the season, attempting to seize supremacy over the Goncourt.

None of the prizes carry a major financal award but they promise an increase in book sales. The Goncourt leads to a surge in sales of about 500,000 extra copies while the Femina usually guarantees about another 100,000.
